questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

I didn't find a dedicated 2025 survey paper on LLM-based requirements elicitation from user reviews. The results are primary studies, which is still useful.

- **App store reviews with fine-tuned LLMs:** One arXiv paper (2409.15473) fine-tuned BERT, DistilBERT, and GEMMA on app reviews labeled for usefulness. BERT performed best, reaching about 92.4% accuracy, and GEMMA had the highest recall (about 93.4%).
- **Usability requirements from reviews (2026):** A precursor study from Leibniz University Hannover (CEUR-WS Vol-4208) tests whether GPT-4.1 can flag usability-related reviews at roughly the level of a human coder, framed within CrowdRE.
- **Stakeholder-facing LLM elicitation (REFSQ 2026):** arXiv 2601.16699 uses LLMs as articulation aids, reformulating stakeholder input. It reports better perceived completeness and clarity, though it doesn't work from reviews.
- **Practitioner survey (SBQS 2025):** A survey of 21 software professionals found that 66.7% of user-story users had adopted LLMs, mostly ChatGPT, for brainstorming and content review.
- **Pipeline case study:** An EGU26 abstract describes an LLM (Llama 3.3) pipeline that clusters and classifies requirements from questionnaires and interview transcripts, with human review.

For a true survey, I'd search arXiv or the IEEE RE and REFSQ proceedings directly for terms like "LLM4RE survey" or "systematic literature review large language models requirements engineering."

Flow's $23M Series A was led by Sequoia, and Rivian is its best-documented customer. The results don't say what Sequoia required as a condition of investing.

- **The round:** Flow announced a $23M Series A, led by Sequoia in October 2025. Sequoia partner Roelof Botha later personally invested and joined Flow's board as an independent director. The round also drew Odyssey Ventures and Patrick and John Collison, per Fenwick's deal announcement.
- **What Flow does:** The company describes its platform as a connected 'systems graph' that keeps requirements, CAD, code, simulations, tests, and certification artifacts in one live system of record.
- **Rivian's adoption:** Rivian integrated the central, AI-powered system of the Sequoia-backed platform Flow to manage all engineering requirements for both R1 and R2 vehicle production. Rivian's evaluation needed a platform that could scale to over 1 million requirements across hardware and software and to support 1,000 concurrent users without lagging. It also had to allow for the transition from existing tools without disrupting production. Flow said the rollout was staged, with programs transitioned one by one.
- **Growth after the Series A:** A later $50M Series B at a $750M valuation reported that adoption at Rivian increased from 40 to 1,500 users within seven months. That round also named an AI harness allowing frontier models to work securely with sensitive engineering data on active hardware programs as a planned use of funds.

Sources conflict on details. One lists Rivian at over 1,000 engineers, while the Series B report cites about 1,500 users. The results also give different founding years (2016 and 2023). These are company-reported figures, so treat them as approximate.

OpenReq was a Horizon 2020 project that built open-source tools for requirements engineering, with release planning as one of its main use cases.

- **Goal:** The project set out to build an open-source requirements management platform with recommender, decision-support, and dependency-management features. It planned to develop, evaluate, and disseminate a fully integrated open-source requirements management platform and a set of connectors.
- **Recommenders:** Its personal recommender component implements advanced recommendation and machine-learning algorithms to assist requirements work, improve a requirement's quality, estimate its properties or predict relevant stakeholders.
- **Prioritization and release planning:** Its group decision support component covers stakeholders' participation, the resolution of preference conflicts, and the identification of consensus, e.g. during release planning. The project also asked how much effort a requirement would cost and in which release it should be delivered.
- **Dependencies:** A dependency management component semi-automatically identifies requirements dependencies, supports requirements reasoning and reuse of requirements knowledge.
- **Later reporting:** Its period-2 report describes tools that bundle sets of these services to demonstrate their capabilities in RE processes like group decision-making, release planning, and user feedback analytics. The project's services were delivered as open source solutions.
- **Research papers:** An ECAI 2020 paper by Samer, Stettinger, Felfernig, Franch, and Falkner presents a variety of innovative recommendation tools developed within the scope of the European Horizon 2020 research project OPENREQ.

The search did not return the project's end date or the repository links, so check CORDIS and the project's publications for those.

- **The deal:** Amplitude's press release, dated July 10, 2025, says it bought Kraftful, an AI-native Voice of Customer startup, to add qualitative feedback alongside its behavioral analytics (investors.amplitude.com).

**Simile** is the best-documented recent raise in this space. Reports from August 2026 say it raised $200M in Series B funding led by Greenoaks at a $2B valuation. That came just five months after a $100 million Series A, which closed on February 12, 2026, led by Index Ventures partner Shardul Shah. The company describes its product as "agentic twins" used to test decisions before real-world rollout. One report says revenue grew 5x in five months, though I'd treat that as company-reported. Its approach is to train a proprietary foundation model on consented interviews and behavioral data, which it contrasts with competitors that rely on prompt-engineered personas without real data grounding.

**Aaru** is described as an AI synthetic research startup that provides near-instant customer research by simulating user behavior. Its valuation reporting is inconsistent. TechCrunch's sourced report says some equity was acquired at a $1 billion valuation, while a lower valuation for other investors resulted in a blended valuation below $1 billion. Another summary puts it at $50M Series A in December 2025 at a $1B valuation.

**Caveats:** Simile's performance data hasn't been published. One analysis notes that the company has not published performance data for that model in its funding announcement. Industry skepticism also persists: only 8% of researchers fully trust synthetic alternatives, per one report. Some coverage also labels the August round a Series B while others describe it as following the Series A, so the round naming varies by source.

**Productboard Spark (announced June 22, 2026)**

- **Agents:** Spark runs specialized agents for distinct product jobs, such as voice-of-customer analysis, codebase understanding, competitive research, and spec writing. The agents share context, and teams can save repeatable workflows as shareable, schedulable Skills.

- **Evidence and citations:** Spark is designed so outputs are traceable. Each insight or recommendation links to its source, such as a customer note or feedback thread. The article states: "Every insight, every recommendation links back to a real customer note."

- **Prioritization:** Spark Home shows a ranked list of opportunities built from customer problems and enriched with strategic and competitive context (Beta). Users can open the supporting evidence and start a spec from there. The article doesn't explain how the ranking works.

- **Human-in-the-loop:** Spark previews every edit before saving changes to Productboard entities. Spec generation is conversational, so users work through feedback and findings with Spark. The article also says: "If you can't put your name on it in front of your VP, Spark doesn't ship it."

- **Audit trail:** The article doesn't mention an audit trail, change log, or logging features. It describes Spark as remembering decisions, signals, and specs over time, but it doesn't say whether those actions are recorded for review.

## Open

### Q-027 — Continuous data intake instead of fixed checkpoints (future)
- Owner: Atahan · not blocking · raised 2026-10-11
- Atahan: the two fixed checkpoints (D-040) will eventually go; new data should be digested automatically — e.g. a background agent that searches the web from time to time, and the user uploading new data into the knowledge base.

### Q-026 — Gaps in the checkpoint research (D-040)
- The agents' web-search quota ran out mid-run. Missing: China model-level sales (5 Series LWB / E-Class L / A6L; Gasgoo/CPCA rankings blocked), Japan & Korea market totals, UK/EU-wide model rankings (Dataforce/JATO), Genesis/Lincoln H1 2026, BMW 1/7 Series volumes in EU/CN, Chinese vs foreign brand share in China, China subsidy pauses, Germany EV-subsidy uptake, UK ZEV mandate, charging-cost vs fuel, in-car AI adoption data, OTA/subscriptions. Full list: `gaps` in `research/checkpoints/checkpoints.json`.
- **China round 2 done (2026-10-11):** +207 items (china_models, china_market, china_context): FY2025/H1 2026 retail for A6L / E-Class / 5 Series, luxury registrations 7 Series / S-Class / S800 / Maybach S, domestic-brand share 64→69 %, luxury retail −30 % in H1, CPCA forecast cut, trade-in fund, L2/NOA standard, McKinsey 2026. Many China model figures are Yiche sums (T3, unverified). Still open: i7 China, BBA combined share, rear-screen/massage penetration, Roland Berger/Bain, Gasgoo (blocked).

### Q-025 — 3D models for the Cars screen (D-039)
- Owner: Atahan · not blocking (placeholder car renders without them)
- Context: the Cars screen renders public, fan-made CC BY Sketchfab models (attribution on screen): 1 Series "Bmw-1-series 2025" (teenlin3, AI-generated mesh, 500k tris), 5 Series "i5" (akyolefe319), 7 Series "2023 BMW I7 G70" (NazhDesign). Downloads need a Sketchfab login (the agent may not log in), so the files must be placed in `data/models/{f70,g60,g70}.glb` (or `<name>/scene.gltf`). Each model's axis orientation in `car_zones.MODELS_GLTF` is provisional until checked visually. For real use BMW would supply its own visualisation assets.

Remaining: whether to keep these fan-made models for the pitch (the 1 Series mesh is AI-generated) and the originals in `challange information document/` can be deleted by Atahan.

### Q-005 — How are the "Source A–D" feedback channels interpreted?
- Owner: team (ask BMW mentors)
- Context: Sources are anonymized. Observed patterns (`documents/data-inventory.md` §1) are hypotheses only:
  - **A:** multi-country (incl. JP/KR), lower-case normalized, possibly translated.
  - **B:** US only, third-person "Customer stated…" notes.
  - **C:** US only, structured survey prompts ("I had a minor/serious problem…", "What is…"), mostly Difficult-to-Use/Defect.
  - **D:** US only; short; unclassified. Two prompt templates in G60 (checked 2026-10-10): 34 of 136 end with "That is the one thing could be most improved about the <area> of my vehicle" (improvement answers, e.g. "the head rests are too short"); the rest are mostly "love the…" answers. So D mixes "what do you like" and "what could be most improved" — the earlier note that D is **not** improvement feedback was wrong.
- This affects source-trust weighting. Don't weight sources differently until confirmed.

Q-027
- 2026-10-11 — Full-screen 2D pages (D-056): Document, AI agents, Audit no longer drawn over the 3D scene; canvas hidden + paused (`frameloop="never"`, stays mounted), timeline hidden there, Document got its own checkpoint switch. Checked in the browser (3D resumes on return).
- 2026-10-12 — Wave pipeline retired (D-057): 8 old API routers, `pipeline/`, `service.py`, `research/findings.py`, old tests/scripts, `logView`, LangGraph removed; shared helpers moved byte-identical (`bmw_req/audit.py`, `prioritize/factors.py`, `prioritize/fitcheck.py`, `structure/taxonomy.py`, `structure/galaxy.py`); `/api/health`. 114 tests, all green.
- 2026-10-12 — Old wave tables dropped (D-058): verified backup `data/backups/app-before-D058-20261012T024059Z.db`, 11 tables dropped in one transaction + audit event + VACUUM (373 → 366 MB), schema no longer creates them; rehearsed on a copy first; app healthy, all screens load. 114 tests green.
- 2026-10-12 — Database direction: Postgres 17 + pgvector, no graph DB (Atahan). Migration plan written (`documents/postgres-migration.md`, D-059 proposed): P0 infra → P1 switch → P2 Postgres features → P3 ops/docs. Waiting for Atahan's approval of the plan.

# Market landscape — evidence-to-requirements & product decision tools

_Researched 2026-10-12 (web search). Purpose: who else works in this space if SharkSight is generalized beyond BMW into a tool anyone can use for ground-up requirements engineering and product decisions. Most sources are vendor pages or vendor-written comparisons, so funding, customer and feature claims are **company-reported** unless noted. Features not checked are marked as such._

## TL;DR

- **Nobody covers the whole chain end to end.** SharkSight's chain is: raw evidence (feedback, studies, sales, web) → findings → measurable requirements → fit/feasibility gates → explainable per-segment priority → human decision → append-only audit, re-run over time. The market splits into tools that stop at **"themes / opportunities"** (feedback intelligence, PM suites) and tools that start from **requirements someone has already written** (requirements management / ALM, systems engineering).
- **Closest threat from above: Productboard Spark** (June 2026). Agents for voice of customer, competitive research, prioritization and specs. Every insight links back to a customer note, and edits are previewed before they are saved. Its ranking logic is not explained, and the launch post mentions no audit trail.
- **Closest threat from below: Flow Engineering.** An AI-native "systems graph" for hardware teams; Rivian uses it for all R1/R2 requirements. It raised a $50M Series B at a $750M valuation on 2026-10-02. Flow starts at engineering requirements, not at customer evidence.
- **Consolidation is fast.** Amplitude bought Kraftful (Jul 2025), Atlassian bought Cycle (Sep 2025) for Jira Product Discovery, and Altium bought Valispace (2023/24). Feedback-to-insight is becoming a feature inside larger suites.
- **Where we could win:** traceable, auditable, segment-aware requirements for **physical / long-cycle / regulated products** (automotive, industrial, medtech, aerospace, consumer hardware). Here the decision is expensive, the PM must defend it, and the SaaS-oriented feedback tools don't fit well.

## 1. Our chain, stated generically

| Step | SharkSight today (BMW) | Generic form |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | verbatims, customer study, sales, option lists, cited web research (T1–T3) | any feedback + quantitative studies + market data + web research, with provenance |
| Findings | clusters, insights, themes, evidence graph | same |
| Requirements | customer-experienced metric + target ladder, horizon, Kano, evidence vs. assumption | same, domain-agnostic |
| Gates | brand & segment fit, platform/plant feasibility | pluggable gates (brand, feasibility, compliance, strategy) |
| Prioritization | prio-v1 per requirement × line × market, factor breakdown, bundles | per requirement × product line × segment |
| Decision | PM approves / rejects / defers with rationale; AI only proposes | same |
| Audit & continuity | append-only `audit_event`, checkpoints, change proposals | same |

## 2. Landscape by category

### A. Customer-feedback intelligence (upstream; stops at themes)

| Tool | What it does | Where it stops |
|---|---|---|
| **Enterpret** | Adaptive taxonomy over feedback from 50+ channels; launched an "agentic customer intelligence platform" Oct 2025. $20.8M Series A (Dec 2024, Canaan); customers incl. Canva, Notion, Strava. | Insights and alerts; no requirement model, no decision record |
| **Unwrap.ai** | Theme detection over many sources (claims 3,000+ connectors); pushes emerging themes to Slack/email | Same |
| **Dovetail** | Research repository → "customer intelligence platform". July 2026 launch: background agents, **customer "digital twins"** built from what segments said, MCP connectors (Claude, Copilot, Slack, Linear), ISO 42001 | Research synthesis; no prioritization or requirements |
| **Kraftful → Amplitude** | LLM analysis of tickets and app reviews, top requests and complaints; acquired Jul 2025 and folded into product analytics | Part of the analytics suite now |
| **BuildBetter** | Calls, tickets and docs → insights, 100+ integrations | Insights and docs |

### B. Product-management suites with AI (midstream; opportunity → spec)

| Tool | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Productboard Spark** (2026-06-22) | Agents for VoC synthesis, competitive research, prioritization, codebase-grounded PRDs; "every insight links back to a real customer note"; previews edits before saving; ranked opportunities (beta); specs go out via MCP to Claude Code / Codex / Cursor | **Closest overall.** Ranking method not explained; no audit trail mentioned; software-product oriented (codebase grounding) |
| **Jira Product Discovery** (+ **Cycle** acquisition, Sep 2025) | AI organizes feedback and connects it to ideas and delivery; Rovo agents; 20k+ customers | Feedback → ideas inside the Atlassian stack |
| **ChatPRD** | AI PRD writer; bootstrapped; claims 100k+ PMs | Document generation, not evidence |
| Aha!, ProdPad, airfocus, Canny, Pendo | Roadmap / idea tools adding AI on top of a user-maintained structure | AI features not checked in this pass |
| Zeda.io | Feedback → roadmap with revenue scoring | A competitor says it is shutting down in 2026 (unverified) |

### C. Classic requirements management / ALM (downstream; starts from written requirements)

| Tool | AI angle | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Jama Connect** | Advisor (NLP quality checks on wording), Trace Scores | Strong in regulated product development |
| **IBM DOORS Next**, **Siemens Polarion**, **PTC Codebeamer**, **Visure** | Quality checks, test generation, risk scoring (varies) | Incumbents in automotive and aerospace. No native Polarion AI assistant found; a community MCP server exposes Polarion items to LLMs |
| **Modern Requirements (Copilot4DevOps)** | Scores requirement quality against "6 C's", generates user stories, Gherkin and tests inside Azure DevOps | Authoring help, not elicitation from evidence |
| **Dassault CATIA R2026x** | "Generative systems requirement creation"; Virtual Companions (Feb 2026) for requirements alignment | Engineering-side, PLM-bound |

**Common gap:** these tools assume requirements already exist. AI improves wording, traceability and tests, not *which* requirements customers need.

### D. AI-native systems engineering (downstream, newer)

| Tool | Facts |
|---|---|
| **Flow Engineering** | "Systems graph" linking requirements, CAD, code, simulations, tests and certification. Agents log changes, flag downstream effects and check requirement and test coverage. Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it (scaled to ~1,500 users in 7 months). Series A $23M (Sequoia, Oct 2025); Series B $50M at $750M (Valor / Atreides, 2026-10-02). |
| **Trace.Space** (Riga) | "AI-native requirements management": trace graph from PDFs, Jira, Git and Confluence; change impact, duplicate detection, standards compliance. $4M seed (Cherry Ventures, Feb 2025). |
| **Valispace** (Altium) | AI-assisted systems and requirements engineering for hardware; acquired by Altium (Dec 2023 / 2024). |

These are the natural **hand-off target** for our output (customer requirements → engineering requirements), not direct competitors.

### E. Market & competitive intelligence (the web-evidence layer)

**Crayon**, **Klue** (Gartner 2026 MQ Leaders for competitive and market intelligence) and **AlphaSense** (financial and strategic research, 500M+ documents). They feed sales and strategy teams. None turns competitive facts into requirements.

### F. Preference research & synthetic customers (the "how much do they want it" layer)

- **Qualtrics**, **Conjointly**, **Quantilope**, **OpinionX**: conjoint, MaxDiff and Kano studies; AI mostly helps with survey building and text analysis.
- **Synthetic customers:** **Simile** ($100M Series A Feb 2026, $200M Series B Aug 2026 at $2B; "agentic twins" trained on consented interviews) and **Aaru** (~$1B valuation). Plus Dovetail's digital twins. Trust is still low (one report: 8% of researchers fully trust synthetic alternatives). For us this is a possible *future-needs* input, but it should be labelled an **assumption, not evidence** (rule 4).

### G. Decision-intelligence platforms (adjacent, different job)

The first Gartner MQ for Decision Intelligence Platforms came out on 2026-01-26. Leaders per vendor releases: Quantexa, FICO, IBM; also Aera, o9, Pega, SAS and others. These platforms cover **operational, repeated decisions** (credit, supply chain, fraud), not one-off product-portfolio decisions. They are still useful vocabulary: governance, explainability, decision records.

### H. Industry services (automotive)

**J.D. Power** brings customer voice into OEM strategy and development, assigning requirements and priorities per vehicle system (consulting plus data such as AutoPlanner). **NTT Data** offers GenAI VoC agents (RAG + knowledge graphs) for automotive. These are services, not self-serve software, so BMW-like customers currently **buy this as consulting**.

### I. Research & open source

- **OpenReq** (EU H2020, 2017–2020): open-source RE platform with recommenders, **group decision support for release planning**, dependency detection and user-feedback analytics. It is the closest academic ancestor of what we do.
- **LLM4RE literature:** a systematic review of 74 studies (arXiv 2509.11446) finds a +136% jump in studies in 2024. Focus is shifting to elicitation and validation, mostly with app-store reviews. No end-to-end evidence → decision systems were reported.
- **StrictDoc, Doorstop, sphinx-needs:** docs-as-code requirements tools (text + Git traceability). They could serve as an export target.

## 3. White space — what nobody else combines

1. **Requirements built from evidence, not just "insights".** A measurable customer-experienced metric, a target ladder (baseline / threshold / target / stretch), and every number tagged cited / projected / assumption / gap. Feedback tools stop before this; RM tools start after it.
2. **Mixed evidence with provenance and trust tiers.** Internal feedback, quantitative studies, sales and cited web research in one evidence graph, with conflicts surfaced (e.g. BMW vs public sales figures).
3. **Segment-aware prioritization.** The same requirement is scored per product line × market, and cross-market conflicts are shown. SaaS tools mostly rank globally or by revenue.
4. **Explainable, deterministic scoring.** A factor breakdown the PM can re-weight. Spark's ranking is opaque in public material.
5. **Decision governance.** The AI only proposes; humans decide with a rationale; append-only audit; snapshots over time. Spark previews edits, but no tool here offers a decision record built for review by others.
6. **Fit / feasibility gates.** Brand fit and platform feasibility generalize to pluggable gates: brand, manufacturability, regulation, strategy.
7. **Future-needs projection.** A 3–5-year horizon from past feedback + competitors + trends, kept separate from evidence.

## 4. Implications if we generalize

- **Positioning:** a "decision-grade requirements" layer **between** the VoC tools and the RM/ALM tools. Ingest from Dovetail, Enterpret, Gong, surveys and CSV/xlsx; hand off to Jira, Jama, Polarion, Flow and ReqIF/StrictDoc. Integrate with both sides instead of competing with them; MCP connectors are now table stakes (Spark, Dovetail and Crayon all ship them).
- **Beachhead:** long-cycle physical products where decisions are costly and must be defended: automotive OEMs and suppliers, industrial equipment, medtech, consumer electronics. Today they rely on consulting (J.D. Power-style) plus spreadsheets.
- **What to make configurable** (largely in line with AGENTS rule 7):
  - brand / model / market → organization / product line / segment
  - brand-fit and plant/platform checks → a gate plug-in interface
  - the 3D car → an optional product visualizer, with a 2D fallback
  - BMW file loaders → a generic ingest with column mapping
  - taxonomy / aspect space → a per-domain template
- **Risks:**
  - Productboard or Atlassian could add audit and segment scoring.
  - Flow could move upstream into customer evidence.
  - LLM synthesis is commoditizing, so the moat has to be the **requirement model, decision governance and integrations**, not the extraction.

# Market landscape — evidence-to-requirements & product decision tools

_Researched 2026-10-12 (web search). Purpose: who else works in this space if SharkSight is generalized beyond BMW into a tool anyone can use for ground-up requirements engineering and product decisions. Most sources are vendor pages or vendor-written comparisons, so funding, customer and feature claims are **company-reported** unless noted. Features not checked are marked as such._

## TL;DR

- **Nobody covers the whole chain end to end.** SharkSight's chain is: raw evidence (feedback, studies, sales, web) → findings → measurable requirements → fit/feasibility gates → explainable per-segment priority → human decision → append-only audit, re-run over time. The market splits into tools that stop at **"themes / opportunities"** (feedback intelligence, PM suites) and tools that start from **requirements someone has already written** (requirements management / ALM, systems engineering).
- **Closest threat from above: Productboard Spark** (June 2026). Agents for voice of customer, competitive research, prioritization and specs. Every insight links back to a customer note, and edits are previewed before they are saved. Its ranking logic is not explained, and the launch post mentions no audit trail.
- **Closest threat from below: Flow Engineering.** An AI-native "systems graph" for hardware teams; Rivian uses it for all R1/R2 requirements. It raised a $50M Series B at a $750M valuation on 2026-10-02. Flow starts at engineering requirements, not at customer evidence.
- **Consolidation is fast.** Amplitude bought Kraftful (Jul 2025), Atlassian bought Cycle (Sep 2025) for Jira Product Discovery, and Altium bought Valispace (2023/24). Feedback-to-insight is becoming a feature inside larger suites.
- **Where we could win:** traceable, auditable, segment-aware requirements for **physical / long-cycle / regulated products** (automotive, industrial, medtech, aerospace, consumer hardware). Here the decision is expensive, the PM must defend it, and the SaaS-oriented feedback tools don't fit well.

## 1. Our chain, stated generically

| Step | SharkSight today (BMW) | Generic form |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | verbatims, customer study, sales, option lists, cited web research (T1–T3) | any feedback + quantitative studies + market data + web research, with provenance |
| Findings | clusters, insights, themes, evidence graph | same |
| Requirements | customer-experienced metric + target ladder, horizon, Kano, evidence vs. assumption | same, domain-agnostic |
| Gates | brand & segment fit, platform/plant feasibility | pluggable gates (brand, feasibility, compliance, strategy) |
| Prioritization | prio-v1 per requirement × line × market, factor breakdown, bundles | per requirement × product line × segment |
| Decision | PM approves / rejects / defers with rationale; AI only proposes | same |
| Audit & continuity | append-only `audit_event`, checkpoints, change proposals | same |

## 2. Landscape by category

### A. Customer-feedback intelligence (upstream; stops at themes)

| Tool | What it does | Where it stops |
|---|---|---|
| **Enterpret** | Adaptive taxonomy over feedback from 50+ channels; launched an "agentic customer intelligence platform" Oct 2025. $20.8M Series A (Dec 2024, Canaan); customers incl. Canva, Notion, Strava. | Insights and alerts; no requirement model, no decision record |
| **Unwrap.ai** | Theme detection over many sources (claims 3,000+ connectors); pushes emerging themes to Slack/email | Same |
| **Dovetail** | Research repository → "customer intelligence platform". July 2026 launch: background agents, **customer "digital twins"** built from what segments said, MCP connectors (Claude, Copilot, Slack, Linear), ISO 42001 | Research synthesis; no prioritization or requirements |
| **Kraftful → Amplitude** | LLM analysis of tickets and app reviews, top requests and complaints; acquired Jul 2025 and folded into product analytics | Part of the analytics suite now |
| **BuildBetter** | Calls, tickets and docs → insights, 100+ integrations | Insights and docs |

### B. Product-management suites with AI (midstream; opportunity → spec)

| Tool | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Productboard Spark** (2026-06-22) | Agents for VoC synthesis, competitive research, prioritization, codebase-grounded PRDs; "every insight links back to a real customer note"; previews edits before saving; ranked opportunities (beta); specs go out via MCP to Claude Code / Codex / Cursor | **Closest overall.** Ranking method not explained; no audit trail mentioned; software-product oriented (codebase grounding) |
| **Jira Product Discovery** (+ **Cycle** acquisition, Sep 2025) | AI organizes feedback and connects it to ideas and delivery; Rovo agents; 20k+ customers | Feedback → ideas inside the Atlassian stack |
| **ChatPRD** | AI PRD writer; bootstrapped; claims 100k+ PMs | Document generation, not evidence |
| Aha!, ProdPad, airfocus, Canny, Pendo | Roadmap / idea tools adding AI on top of a user-maintained structure | AI features not checked in this pass |
| Zeda.io | Feedback → roadmap with revenue scoring | A competitor says it is shutting down in 2026 (unverified) |

### C. Classic requirements management / ALM (downstream; starts from written requirements)

| Tool | AI angle | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Jama Connect** | Advisor (NLP quality checks on wording), Trace Scores | Strong in regulated product development |
| **IBM DOORS Next**, **Siemens Polarion**, **PTC Codebeamer**, **Visure** | Quality checks, test generation, risk scoring (varies) | Incumbents in automotive and aerospace. No native Polarion AI assistant found; a community MCP server exposes Polarion items to LLMs |
| **Modern Requirements (Copilot4DevOps)** | Scores requirement quality against "6 C's", generates user stories, Gherkin and tests inside Azure DevOps | Authoring help, not elicitation from evidence |
| **Dassault CATIA R2026x** | "Generative systems requirement creation"; Virtual Companions (Feb 2026) for requirements alignment | Engineering-side, PLM-bound |

**Common gap:** these tools assume requirements already exist. AI improves wording, traceability and tests, not *which* requirements customers need.

### D. AI-native systems engineering (downstream, newer)

| Tool | Facts |
|---|---|
| **Flow Engineering** | "Systems graph" linking requirements, CAD, code, simulations, tests and certification. Agents log changes, flag downstream effects and check requirement and test coverage. Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it (scaled to ~1,500 users in 7 months). Series A $23M (Sequoia, Oct 2025); Series B $50M at $750M (Valor / Atreides, 2026-10-02). |
| **Trace.Space** (Riga) | "AI-native requirements management": trace graph from PDFs, Jira, Git and Confluence; change impact, duplicate detection, standards compliance. $4M seed (Cherry Ventures, Feb 2025). |
| **Valispace** (Altium) | AI-assisted systems and requirements engineering for hardware; acquired by Altium (Dec 2023 / 2024). |

These are the natural **hand-off target** for our output (customer requirements → engineering requirements), not direct competitors.

### E. Market & competitive intelligence (the web-evidence layer)

**Crayon**, **Klue** (Gartner 2026 MQ Leaders for competitive and market intelligence) and **AlphaSense** (financial and strategic research, 500M+ documents). They feed sales and strategy teams. None turns competitive facts into requirements.

### F. Preference research & synthetic customers (the "how much do they want it" layer)

- **Qualtrics**, **Conjointly**, **Quantilope**, **OpinionX**: conjoint, MaxDiff and Kano studies; AI mostly helps with survey building and text analysis.
- **Synthetic customers:** **Simile** ($100M Series A Feb 2026, $200M Series B Aug 2026 at $2B; "agentic twins" trained on consented interviews) and **Aaru** (~$1B valuation). Plus Dovetail's digital twins. Trust is still low (one report: 8% of researchers fully trust synthetic alternatives). For us this is a possible *future-needs* input, but it should be labelled an **assumption, not evidence** (rule 4).

### G. Decision-intelligence platforms (adjacent, different job)

The first Gartner MQ for Decision Intelligence Platforms came out on 2026-01-26. Leaders per vendor releases: Quantexa, FICO, IBM; also Aera, o9, Pega, SAS and others. These platforms cover **operational, repeated decisions** (credit, supply chain, fraud), not one-off product-portfolio decisions. They are still useful vocabulary: governance, explainability, decision records.

### H. Industry services (automotive)

**J.D. Power** brings customer voice into OEM strategy and development, assigning requirements and priorities per vehicle system (consulting plus data such as AutoPlanner). **NTT Data** offers GenAI VoC agents (RAG + knowledge graphs) for automotive. These are services, not self-serve software, so BMW-like customers currently **buy this as consulting**.

### I. Research & open source

- **OpenReq** (EU H2020, 2017–2020): open-source RE platform with recommenders, **group decision support for release planning**, dependency detection and user-feedback analytics. It is the closest academic ancestor of what we do.
- **LLM4RE literature:** a systematic review of 74 studies (arXiv 2509.11446) finds a +136% jump in studies in 2024. Focus is shifting to elicitation and validation, mostly with app-store reviews. No end-to-end evidence → decision systems were reported.
- **StrictDoc, Doorstop, sphinx-needs:** docs-as-code requirements tools (text + Git traceability). They could serve as an export target.

## 3. White space — what nobody else combines

1. **Requirements built from evidence, not just "insights".** A measurable customer-experienced metric, a target ladder (baseline / threshold / target / stretch), and every number tagged cited / projected / assumption / gap. Feedback tools stop before this; RM tools start after it.
2. **Mixed evidence with provenance and trust tiers.** Internal feedback, quantitative studies, sales and cited web research in one evidence graph, with conflicts surfaced (e.g. BMW vs public sales figures).
3. **Segment-aware prioritization.** The same requirement is scored per product line × market, and cross-market conflicts are shown. SaaS tools mostly rank globally or by revenue.
4. **Explainable, deterministic scoring.** A factor breakdown the PM can re-weight. Spark's ranking is opaque in public material.
5. **Decision governance.** The AI only proposes; humans decide with a rationale; append-only audit; snapshots over time. Spark previews edits, but no tool here offers a decision record built for review by others.
6. **Fit / feasibility gates.** Brand fit and platform feasibility generalize to pluggable gates: brand, manufacturability, regulation, strategy.
7. **Future-needs projection.** A 3–5-year horizon from past feedback + competitors + trends, kept separate from evidence.

## 4. Implications if we generalize

- **Positioning:** a "decision-grade requirements" layer **between** the VoC tools and the RM/ALM tools. Ingest from Dovetail, Enterpret, Gong, surveys and CSV/xlsx; hand off to Jira, Jama, Polarion, Flow and ReqIF/StrictDoc. Integrate with both sides instead of competing with them; MCP connectors are now table stakes (Spark, Dovetail and Crayon all ship them).
- **Beachhead:** long-cycle physical products where decisions are costly and must be defended: automotive OEMs and suppliers, industrial equipment, medtech, consumer electronics. Today they rely on consulting (J.D. Power-style) plus spreadsheets.
- **What to make configurable** (largely in line with AGENTS rule 7):
  - brand / model / market → organization / product line / segment
  - brand-fit and plant/platform checks → a gate plug-in interface
  - the 3D car → an optional product visualizer, with a 2D fallback
  - BMW file loaders → a generic ingest with column mapping
  - taxonomy / aspect space → a per-domain template
- **Risks:**
  - Productboard or Atlassian could add audit and segment scoring.
  - Flow could move upstream into customer evidence.
  - LLM synthesis is commoditizing, so the moat has to be the **requirement model, decision governance and integrations**, not the extraction.
  - Enterprise customers need data controls (redaction, no training on their data, ISO 42001-style certification is becoming expected).

Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it (scaled to ~1,500 users in 7 months). Series A $23M (Sequoia, Oct 2025); Series B $50M at $750M (Valor / Atreides, 2026-10-02). |
| **Trace.Space** (Riga) | "AI-native requirements management": trace graph from PDFs, Jira, Git and Confluence; change impact, duplicate detection, standards compliance. $4M seed (Cherry Ventures, Feb 2025). |
| **Valispace** (Altium) | AI-assisted systems and requirements engineering for hardware; acquired by Altium (Dec 2023 / 2024). |

These are the natural **hand-off target** for our output (customer requirements → engineering requirements), not direct competitors.

### E. Market & competitive intelligence (the web-evidence layer)

**Crayon**, **Klue** (Gartner 2026 MQ Leaders for competitive and market intelligence) and **AlphaSense** (financial and strategic research, 500M+ documents). They feed sales and strategy teams. None turns competitive facts into requirements.

### F. Preference research & synthetic customers (the "how much do they want it" layer)

- **Qualtrics**, **Conjointly**, **Quantilope**, **OpinionX**: conjoint, MaxDiff and Kano studies; AI mostly helps with survey building and text analysis.
- **Synthetic customers:** **Simile** ($100M Series A Feb 2026, $200M Series B Aug 2026 at $2B; "agentic twins" trained on consented interviews) and **Aaru** (~$1B valuation). Plus Dovetail's digital twins. Trust is still low (one report: 8% of researchers fully trust synthetic alternatives). For us this is a possible *future-needs* input, but it should be labelled an **assumption, not evidence** (rule 4).

### G. Decision-intelligence platforms (adjacent, different job)

The first Gartner MQ for Decision Intelligence Platforms came out on 2026-01-26. Leaders per vendor releases: Quantexa, FICO, IBM; also Aera, o9, Pega, SAS and others. These platforms cover **operational, repeated decisions** (credit, supply chain, fraud), not one-off product-portfolio decisions. They are still useful vocabulary: governance, explainability, decision records.

### H. Industry services (automotive)

**J.D. Power** brings customer voice into OEM strategy and development, assigning requirements and priorities per vehicle system (consulting plus data such as AutoPlanner). **NTT Data** offers GenAI VoC agents (RAG + knowledge graphs) for automotive. These are services, not self-serve software, so BMW-like customers currently **buy this as consulting**.

### I. Research & open source

- **OpenReq** (EU H2020, 2017–2020): open-source RE platform with recommenders, **group decision support for release planning**, dependency detection and user-feedback analytics. It is the closest academic ancestor of what we do.
- **LLM4RE literature:** a systematic review of 74 studies (arXiv 2509.11446) finds a +136% jump in studies in 2024. Focus is shifting to elicitation and validation, mostly with app-store reviews. No end-to-end evidence → decision systems were reported.
- **StrictDoc, Doorstop, sphinx-needs:** docs-as-code requirements tools (text + Git traceability). They could serve as an export target.

## 3. White space — what nobody else combines

1. **Requirements built from evidence, not just "insights".** A measurable customer-experienced metric, a target ladder (baseline / threshold / target / stretch), and every number tagged cited / projected / assumption / gap. Feedback tools stop before this; RM tools start after it.
2. **Mixed evidence with provenance and trust tiers.** Internal feedback, quantitative studies, sales and cited web research in one evidence graph, with conflicts surfaced (e.g. BMW vs public sales figures).
3. **Segment-aware prioritization.** The same requirement is scored per product line × market, and cross-market conflicts are shown. SaaS tools mostly rank globally or by revenue.
4. **Explainable, deterministic scoring.** A factor breakdown the PM can re-weight. Spark's ranking is opaque in public material.
5. **Decision governance.** The AI only proposes; humans decide with a rationale; append-only audit; snapshots over time. Spark previews edits, but no tool here offers a decision record built for review by others.
6. **Fit / feasibility gates.** Brand fit and platform feasibility generalize to pluggable gates: brand, manufacturability, regulation, strategy.
7. **Future-needs projection.** A 3–5-year horizon from past feedback + competitors + trends, kept separate from evidence.

## 4. Implications if we generalize

- **Positioning:** a "decision-grade requirements" layer **between** the VoC tools and the RM/ALM tools. Ingest from Dovetail, Enterpret, Gong, surveys and CSV/xlsx; hand off to Jira, Jama, Polarion, Flow and ReqIF/StrictDoc. Integrate with both sides instead of competing with them; MCP connectors are now table stakes (Spark, Dovetail and Crayon all ship them).
- **Beachhead:** long-cycle physical products where decisions are costly and must be defended: automotive OEMs and suppliers, industrial equipment, medtech, consumer electronics. Today they rely on consulting (J.D. Power-style) plus spreadsheets.
- **What to make configurable** (largely in line with AGENTS rule 7):
  - brand / model / market → organization / product line / segment
  - brand-fit and plant/platform checks → a gate plug-in interface
  - the 3D car → an optional product visualizer, with a 2D fallback
  - BMW file loaders → a generic ingest with column mapping
  - taxonomy / aspect space → a per-domain template
- **Risks:**
  - Productboard or Atlassian could add audit and segment scoring.
  - Flow could move upstream into customer evidence.
  - LLM synthesis is commoditizing, so the moat has to be the **requirement model, decision governance and integrations**, not the extraction.
  - Enterprise customers need data controls (redaction, no training on their data, ISO 42001-style certification is becoming expected).

content.text:
I've finished the market scan and saved it to `research/market-landscape.md`, with about 20 tools across 9 categories and a source list. Most of what I found comes from vendor pages, so the funding, customer and feature details are mostly what the companies say about themselves.

**Main finding:** no tool I found covers the whole chain SharkSight does: evidence → findings → measurable requirements → fit/feasibility gates → priority by market or segment → a human decides → append-only audit trail, re-run over time. The market splits in two:

- **Tools that stop at "themes" or "opportunities"**: Enterpret, Unwrap, Dovetail (which added AI customer "digital twins" in July 2026), Kraftful (now part of Amplitude), and Jira Product Discovery (Atlassian bought Cycle for it).
- **Tools that start from requirements someone has already written**: Jama, DOORS, Polarion, Codebeamer, Visure, Modern Requirements, Dassault CATIA. Their AI mostly improves wording, traceability and test generation; it doesn't decide *which* requirements customers need.

**Closest competitors:**
- **Productboard Spark** (June 2026) comes from the upstream side. It has agents for customer feedback, competitive research, prioritization and product specs, and every insight links back to a customer note. But its public material doesn't explain how it ranks things, mentions no audit trail, and it's built around software products.
- **Flow Engineering** comes from the downstream side. It's an AI-native engineering platform; Rivian runs all R1/R2 requirements on it, and it raised a $50M Series B at a $750M valuation on 2 Oct 2026. It starts at engineering requirements, not customer evidence, so it's more of a hand-off target than a rival.

**Adjacent areas** that feed into or border on this: competitive intelligence (Crayon, Klue, AlphaSense), survey-based preference research (Qualtrics, Conjointly) and AI-simulated customers (Simile at $2B, Aaru). Further out are "decision intelligence" platforms, which handle repeated operational decisions like credit or fraud, and automotive consulting (J.D. Power, NTT Data). The closest academic predecessor is the EU's OpenReq project.

**What this means for a general version:**
- **Positioning:** a layer *between* customer-feedback tools and requirements/engineering tools. It would take in data from Dovetail, Enterpret, surveys or spreadsheets and hand off to Jira, Jama, Polarion, Flow or the ReqIF exchange format. Connectors that let AI assistants read the data are now standard.
- **First market:** physical, long-cycle or regulated products (automotive, industrial, medtech, hardware). Decisions there are expensive and have to be defended, and today they're mostly made with consultants and spreadsheets.
- **What protects you:** the requirement model (measurable targets, evidence kept separate from assumptions), explainable scoring per segment, and the decision governance. Turning feedback into insights with an LLM is becoming a commodity, so the AI extraction alone won't set you apart.

Following the project rules, I logged this as an open question (**Q-028**) in `foundation/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` and added a line to the session log in `foundation/STATE.md`; no decisions were recorded. Nothing is committed. There are also uncommitted changes in the working tree that I didn't make (Postgres/Alembic files, `Makefile`, `compose.yaml`, and others), so I left them alone.

I can also turn this into a shareable web page if you want to pass it around.
